content.text:
The learner is **part-based**. I submitted that verdict with confidence 0.93, and used 9 of the 60 budget.

**Design:** I trained only two tasks, `L1-S1-M1` and `L2-S2-M2`, so each rule appeared in exactly one trained task. A factor-when-justified learner needs a rule in at least 2 trained tasks before it becomes a reusable part. So at this point it would have no parts yet and would behave like the holistic learner. That leaves one comparison that separates the hypotheses: a task made only of trained rules but unlike any trained task, versus a task with a new rule that closely resembles a trained task.

| Test task | New rules | Highest similarity to a trained task | Examples to criterion |
|---|---|---|---|
| `L2-S1-M1` | 0 | 0.50 | 1, 1 |
| `L2-S1-M2` | 0 | 0.625 | 1 |
| `L1-S1-M4` | 1 | 0.75 | 18, 17 |
| `L3-S3-M3` | 3 | 0.19 | 34, 36 |

The cost went up by about 17 examples for each new rule, whatever the similarity. The recombined tasks were learned almost at once even though they look unlike anything trained. A holistic learner, or a factor-when-justified learner with no parts yet, would have learned the similar task `L1-S1-M4` fastest.

The remaining doubt comes from the small sample. Each task was tested only once or twice, though the repeats agreed closely.
